extracted.intended_audience: military officers, Judge Advocate General staff, War Department legal advisors, and administrators interpreting Army regulations
extracted.subtask_description: Compilation of legal rulings and interpretive guidance on the application of statutes and Army regulations governing subsistence, medical practice, appointments, duties, and the use of the Army in civil matters. Useful for legal advisors and military administrators applying statutory and regulatory limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of forage/subsistence to retired officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Sales of forage, sold at cost price and authorized to be made to "officers of the Army" are not restricted by statute to officers on the active list; therefore sale of forage to retired officers at cost price is legally permissible subject to restrictions as to amount and conditions imposed by the Secretary of War.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such sales 'stand on precisely the same footing, in respect to legality, as the sale of subsistence' to retired officers. Legislative sanction unnecessary where statute already authorizes sales to 'officers of the Army.' (C. 19126, Apr. 12, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability of mess members vs. commercial partnership
rubrics_metrics.description: A mess of three officers charged with subsistence by a post commissary is not in the nature of a commercial partnership; each member is bound to the United States only for his proportion (one-third) of the account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one member pays another who acted as caterer and that caterer dies without paying the commissary, the paying member remains liable to the United States for his one-third proportion. (R. 41, 155, Mar., 1878.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Issuance of stores beyond established rations unlawful
rubrics_metrics.description: The issue of stores for food beyond amounts fixed in established rations is not lawful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct holding: issuance beyond established ration amounts is unauthorized. (C. 6728, July 21, 1899.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractual waiver of ration eligibility rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Where employees (e.g., Alaskan telegraph line employees paid > $60/month) were issued rations because no other method of subsistence was practicable and such issue was incorporated into contracts of employment, this constitutes a waiver of Army Regulations par.1219 requirements, and was lawful for the Secretary of War to make.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies when ration issuance is made part of employment contract and no practicable alternative exists. (C. 19366, Mar. 13, 1906 and June 22, 1907.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Issuing rations in kind where other subsistence unavailable
rubrics_metrics.description: Where other subsistence cannot be obtained at places in Alaska, female nurses and enlisted patients in hospital may be issued rations in kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical necessity in remote locations can justify in-kind rations for particular classes. (C. 20184, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on Chief of Ordnance authority under §1167 R.S.
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1167, R.S., does not direct or authorize the Chief of Ordnance, even with Secretary approval, to draw up and enforce within his department a system of rules and regulations for inspection of ordnance property with a view to its condemnation and sale or destruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory language does not permit such independent regulatory scheme in ordnance department. (C. 63, July, 1894.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination requirements for line officers detailed to Ordnance
rubrics_metrics.description: A line officer detailed for service in the Ordnance Department under the act of June 25, 1906, is required to take the examination for promotion in the line as provided in the act of October 1, 1890; however, under General Order 220 the principle of equivalency may excuse examination in branches where he previously passed successful examinations for detail in Ordnance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalency principles may apply to exempt certain branch examinations, subject to existing promotion orders. (C. 22432, Dec. 2, 1907.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Second detail fitness verification is not an 'examination'
rubrics_metrics.description: Verification of capacity and fitness for a second detail in the Ordnance Department, as per act of June 25, 1906, depends on recommendation of a board of ordnance officers and is not an 'examination' in the sense used by acts regulating advancement of officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus General Order 220 does not exempt ordnance officers from existing examination orders for promotion in their line. (C. 22432, Dec. 2, 1907.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 1765 R.S. does not bar outside compensation when unrelated
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1765, R.S., does not prohibit payment of compensation to an ordnance sergeant for work (e.g., as 'time keeper') under the U.S. Engineer Department where that employment has no connection with the line of his official duty as ordnance sergeant and does not interfere with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-affinity and non-interference with official duties are key to allowing outside compensation. (C. 2670, Sept., 1896.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Engineer Department duties constrained by congressional enactments
rubrics_metrics.description: Duties of the Engineer Department relating to canals, river and harbor improvements, fortifications and seacoast defenses are carried on under direction of the Secretary of War and Chief of Engineers, whose authority is measured by Congress's enactments prescribing duties and responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjutant General's role limited to certain administrative record duties when station changes, leave, or retirement arise. (C. 25730, Oct. 30, 1909.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical practice by Army Medical Corps officers outside posts
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical practice by officers of the Medical Corps outside military posts should conform to State laws, except that medical treatment of members of the Army on the active list, being an instrumentality of the U.S. Government, cannot be controlled by State legislation and may be furnished wherever the soldier is stationed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enlisted men on the retired list are allowed medical attendance at stations of medical officers only. Medical officers on duty are required to attend officers and enlisted men and, when practicable, their families; attendance on families or civilians outside military reservations must comply with State laws. (G. 3270, June, 1899; 20396, Sept. 18, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Board of review jurisdiction limited by statute forbidding second examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Where law expressly provides that 'a second examination shall not be allowed,' a board of review's jurisdiction is restricted to the record of the original examining board (including all documentary and testimonial evidence submitted); taking new testimony would be in the nature of a prohibited second examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board of review cannot conduct independent inquiry beyond original record. (a. 23135, June 12, 1908.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary of War's role regarding board of review findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the act of April 23, 1908, the Secretary of War appoints the board reviewing original examinations of Medical Corps officers, but is not required to approve or disapprove its findings; the department's action upon the board's findings is ministerial (executing discharges, advancing entitled officers, and announcing results).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings become operative from date of publication; Secretary's role is execution rather than discretionary re‑evaluation. (C. 23135, June 24, 1908.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and determination of 'emergency' for Medical Reserve Corps activation
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'emergency' (authorizing ordering Medical Reserve Corps officers to active duty) lacks a rigorous exact definition; it denotes an unforeseen occasion or pressing necessity and is to be determined by the Surgeon General, whose conclusion, when approved by the Secretary of War, is decisive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: vacancy of contract surgeon at post or necessity of services at a post can constitute an emergency warranting activation. Dictionaries cited (Webster, Century) for ordinary meanings. (C. 23135, June 26, 1908.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and dormancy of Medical Reserve Corps commissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Commissions issued to appointees in the Medical Reserve Corps should be drawn to evidence an exercise of appointing power and, as the Corps is part of military establishment, be similar in form to commissions issued to Medical Corps officers, subject to changes restricting operation to periods of active employment; at other times commissions are dormant and vest no authority or duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commissions operate only during active employment; otherwise they confer no rights. (a. 23135, May 8, 1908.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Privileges for Medical Reserve Corps members when not active
rubrics_metrics.description: While as a matter of law only those in active service are entitled to privileges of Army officers, it is proper on principle to extend all privileges not involving official rights to members of the Medical Reserve Corps consistent with their interest in the service, so long as they do not conflict with existing law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle of broad consideration for reserves, but bounded by statutory limits. (C. 23135, Aug. 1, 1908.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of reserve commission does not create pay or leave rights absent assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere acceptance of office in the Medical Reserve Corps, not coupled with assignment to duty, creates no rights to pay, allowances, or leave; assignment to duty places the officer in same leave/pay status as other commissioned officers subject to statutes regulating pay during cumulative leave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignment to duty triggers pay/leave rights; otherwise appointment alone is dormant. (C. 23135, June 29, 1908.)

rubrics_metrics.name: President's power to relieve or discharge reserve officers
rubrics_metrics.description: The President can relieve an officer of the Medical Reserve Corps from duty when services are no longer necessary and may honorably discharge an officer when services are no longer needed; reserve officers are subject to Articles of War and military laws during their period of service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve officers committing criminal offenses while serving are subject to same disciplinary control as other officers. (C. 23135, Dec. 19, 1908.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract surgeons/dental surgeons are civilians, not commissioned officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Contract or acting assistant surgeons and contract dental surgeons are not commissioned officers, have no military rank, and are civilians employed by contract; they are not part of the Army though some military jurisdiction may apply when employed with the Army in the field during war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because employment is contractual, oath of office is not a prerequisite to compensation; contract surgeons may perform many medical administrative tasks but are not eligible for retirement and cannot be compelled to remain beyond contract term. (C. 10566, Nov. 5, 1909; C. 8618, July, 1900; G. citations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Privileges of contract surgeons (purchases, signatures, duties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contract surgeons may buy fuel and forage from quartermaster's department, purchase necessary field equipment, sign surgeons' certificates of disability, prepare and sign final statements, act as post treasurer, and supervise subordinates in hospitals, but they are not entitled to admission to Government Hospital for the Insane and are not eligible for retirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hospital Corps strength and detailing authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The strength of the Hospital Corps was not increased by the act of May 11, 1908, and its strength can only be increased by affirmative action of the Secretary of War under authority vested by the act of March 1, 1887.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sergeants of the first class of Hospital Corps can be detailed as mess sergeants only under special authority of the Surgeon General. (C. 23288, Apr. 15, 1909; C. 23695, Oct. 12, 1909.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Army Nurse Corps status and leave rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The Nurse Corps (female) is an integral part of the U.S. Army for purposes of military service and is not part of the executive civil service subject to civil-service acts; the 30 days' leave of absence provided to female nurses is not cumulative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences for classification and leave administration. (C. 10566, Oct. 13, 1909; C. 10160, May 29, 1902.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility for admission to Army and General hospitals
rubrics_metrics.description: Under regulations for the Army and Navy General Hospital at Hot Springs, civil employees are not eligible for admission; discharged enlisted men within three months of possible reenlistment under certain acts are not entitled to admission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admissions governed by specific hospital regulations and statutory reenlistment windows. (P. 58, 452, Mar., 1893; C. 2069, Feb., 1896.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Officers' household servants entitled to post hospital admission
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers' servants, being part of the officer's household, are equitably entitled to admission to post hospitals and should not be treated the same as 'civilians not in public service.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat servants with same liberality afforded for subsistence supplies purchased for officer's household. (P. 37, 460, Jan., 1890.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Estate of soldier dying without heirs escheats to United States
rubrics_metrics.description: In case of death of a soldier at a post hospital leaving an estate without heirs and without will, the estate escheats to the United States; post surgeon should deposit money with the paymaster to the credit of the United States, taking receipts in duplicate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Army Regulations procedures for deposit and receipts. (C. 20272, Aug. 24, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Special diet appropriations permit purchase of certain items
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriation for special diet for enlisted patients too sick for Army rations reasonably permits purchase of items such as ginger ale and a charged water (Tansan) for the sick.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable interpretation of March 2, 1901 appropriation. (C. 12094, Feb. 27, 1902.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposition funds available to replace medical supplies
rubrics_metrics.description: All moneys arising from dispositions of serviceable medical and hospital supplies constitute one fund available to replace medical and hospital supplies throughout the fiscal year in which dispositions were effected and the following fiscal year; funds reimbursing cost of a safe are available for replacing supplies under that act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation of June 12, 1906 statute on funds arising from disposition of medical supplies. (C. 20993, Jan. 26, 1907.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Army to protect a State from invasion or domestic violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Article IV, section 4 of the Constitution, the Army may be employed to protect a State from 'invasion' or 'domestic violence' only by order of the President made 'on application of the legislature, or of the executive when the legislature cannot be convened.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Military commanders have no authority to furnish troops to a state official without such a presidential order; see many citations (R. 30,125; C. 2063; etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'when the legislature cannot be convened'
rubrics_metrics.description: The proviso 'when the legislature cannot be convened' generally means when it is not in session or cannot be assembled forthwith or in time to provide for the emergency under State law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to determine when a governor's application is adequate for presidential employment of troops. (R. 30, 172; C. 5557; 8383; 22474.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Army to aid civil authorities in Territories (Alaska/Indian Territory)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Territories like Alaska, where a civil government exists and laws of another state are made operative, the President can legally give military assistance to a U.S. marshal to execute process when marshal is unlawfully prevented from doing so; certain statutes and acts may exempt or authorize such use in Territories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Alaska and Indian Territory cases; operation depends on applicable territorial statutes and congressional acts. (C. 3119; C. 3388; R. 53, 272; others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on using Army for civil law enforcement (posse comitatus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Military forces of the U.S. cannot be permitted to serve as part of a sheriff's posse or otherwise be employed to execute local state laws except where Constitution or act of Congress expressly authorizes such employment; in the absence of presidential orders under constitutional or statutory provisions, combined military action to make arrests or prevent breaches of the peace in civil cases is illegal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officers/soldiers may act as citizens to arrest in flagrante delicto but not as military agents without proper orders; violation risks personal responsibility. (Numerous citations: R. 36, 39, 43; C. 11928; 16165; 17508; 20104; 20570; 22360.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential authority under section 5298 R.S. to employ Army to secure execution of process
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a marshal or deputy marshal is prevented from making due service of judicial process by forcible resistance of an unlawful assemblage, the President is expressly authorized under section 5298, R.S., to employ such part of the Army as he deems necessary to secure due service and execute the laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an express statutory exception to the general prohibition on military execution of laws. (R. 39, 665; other cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Philippine Scouts and constabulary command relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: The Philippine Scouts are part of the Military Establishment by statute. Prior to constabulary legislation their status as military organizations constrained their noninterference in civil affairs similarly to other Regular Army organizations; legislation has vested certain constabulary officers with command power over scouts in specified circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extent of use determined by conference between civil and military authorities; applicable statutes cited (act of Feb. 2, 1901; act of July 1, 1902; act of Jan. 30, 1903).
